claim: KCa2.1, KCa2.2, KCa2.3 and KCa3.1 constitute a family of mammalian small- to intermediate-conductance potassium channels that are activated by calcium-calmodulin.
source: KCa2.1, KCa2.2, KCa2.3 and KCa3.1 constitute a family of mammalian small- to intermediate-conductance potassium channels that are activated by calcium-calmodulin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the KCa channel family, supported by the citation to Adelman et al., 2012 in the Introduction.

claim: KCa3.1 activation requires, in addition to calcium, phosphorylation of a single histidine residue (His358) in the cytoplasmic region by nucleoside diphosphate kinase-B (NDPK-B).
source: KCa3.1 is unique among these four channels in that activation requires, in addition to calcium, phosphorylation of a single histidine residue (His358) in the cytoplasmic region, by nucleoside diphosphate kinase-B (NDPK-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript (Di et al., 2010; Srivastava et al., 2006b).

claim: Phosphorylation of His358 activates KCa3.1 by antagonizing copper-mediated inhibition of the channel.
source: Here, we demonstrate that phosphorylation of His358 activates KCa3.1 by antagonizing copper-mediated inhibition of the channel.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells deficient in intracellular copper exhibit increased KCa3.1 histidine phosphorylation and channel activity.
source: Furthermore, we show that activated CD4+ T cells deficient in intracellular copper exhibit increased KCa3.1 histidine phosphorylation and channel activity, leading to increased calcium flux and cytokine production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells deficient in intracellular copper exhibit increased calcium flux and cytokine production.
source: Furthermore, we show that activated CD4+ T cells deficient in intracellular copper exhibit increased KCa3.1 histidine phosphorylation and channel activity, leading to increased calcium flux and cytokine production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: KCa2.1, KCa2.2 and KCa2.3 are expressed predominantly in neurons, contributing to medium afterhyperpolarization.
source: KCa2.1, KCa2.2 and KCa2.3 are expressed predominantly in neurons, contributing to medium afterhyperpolarization
evidence: This is established knowledge about KCa channel expression patterns, supported by the citation to Adelman et al., 2012.

claim: KCa3.1 plays a key role in the activation of T cells, B cells and mast cells.
source: whereas KCa3.1 plays a key role in the activation of T cells, B cells and mast cells (Feske et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feske et al., 2015.

claim: Potassium efflux via KCa3.1 is required to maintain a negative membrane potential, which provides the electrical gradient for sustained calcium influx via calcium release-activated channels (CRACs).
source: Potassium efflux via KCa3.1 is required to maintain a negative membrane potential, which provides the electrical gradient for sustained calcium influx via calcium release-activated channels (CRACs) and subsequent production of cytokines (Feske et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feske et al., 2015.

claim: His358 of KCa3.1 is phosphorylated (pHis358) by nucleoside diphosphate kinase-B (NDPK-B).
source: We showed previously that His358 of KCa3.1 is phosphorylated (pHis358) by nucleoside diphosphate kinase-B (NDPK-B) (Di et al., 2010; Srivastava et al., 2006b)
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: NDPK-A and NDPK-B are the only two mammalian protein histidine kinases identified to date.
source: which, along with NDPK-A, are the only two mammalian protein histidine kinases identified to date (Attwood and Wieland, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Attwood and Wieland, 2015.

claim: KCa3.1 activation requires phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P).
source: We also showed that KCa3.1 activation requires phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) (Srivastava et al., 2006a)
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: PI(3)P is generated by a class II phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K-C2β).
source: generated by a class II phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K-C2β) (Srivastava et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: KCa3.1 is negatively regulated by protein histidine phosphatase-1 (PHPT1), which dephosphorylates pHis358.
source: and that KCa3.1 is negatively regulated by protein histidine phosphatase-1 (PHPT1), which dephosphorylates pHis358 (Srivastava et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: KCa3.1 is negatively regulated by myotubularin-related protein-6 (MTMR6), which dephosphorylates PI(3)P.
source: and by myotubularin-related protein-6 (MTMR6), which dephosphorylates PI(3)P (Srivastava et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphoglycerate mutase-5 (PGAM5) is a histidine phosphatase that specifically dephosphorylates the catalytic histidine (His118) in NDPK-B.
source: In addition, we recently identified phosphoglycerate mutase-5 (PGAM5) as a histidine phosphatase that specifically dephosphorylates the catalytic histidine (His118) in NDPK-B.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript (Panda et al., 2016).

claim: PGAM5 negatively regulates T-cell receptor signaling by inhibiting NDPK-B-mediated histidine phosphorylation and activation of KCa3.1.
source: By dephosphorylating NDPK-B, PGAM5 negatively regulates T-cell receptor signaling by inhibiting NDPK-B-mediated histidine phosphorylation and activation of KCa3.1 (Panda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of His358 (H358N) converted KCa3.1 into a channel that requires only calcium-calmodulin for activation.
source: We reported previously that mutation of His358 (H358N) converted KCa3.1 into a channel that, like the other three KCa channels, requires only calcium-calmodulin for activation (Srivastava et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Swapping 14 residues of KCa3.1 containing His358 with the equivalent residues of KCa2.3 converted KCa2.3 into a channel that required NDPK-B and PI(3)P for activation.
source: Furthermore, swapping 14 residues of KCa3.1 containing His358 with the equivalent residues of KCa2.3 converted the latter into a channel that required NDPK-B and PI(3)P for activation (Srivastava et al., 2006a).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Histidine phosphorylation is well characterized in prokaryotic two-component systems used in chemotaxis and other sensing systems.
source: Although histidine phosphorylation is well characterized in prokaryotic two-component systems used in chemotaxis and other sensing systems (Hess et al., 1988)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hess et al., 1988.

claim: Histidine phosphorylation is poorly characterized in eukaryotes.
source: it is poorly characterized in eukaryotes (Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009.

claim: Phosphohistidine is more labile than phosphotyrosine or phosphoserine/threonine.
source: in part because phosphohistidine is more labile than phosphotyrosine or phosphoserine/threonine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical properties of phosphohistidine.

claim: Histidine phosphorylation of the β subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins by NDPKs has been reported.
source: In addition to KCa3.1, histidine phosphorylation of several mammalian proteins by NDPKs has been reported, including the β subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins and the transient receptor potential vanilloid-5 (TRPV5) channel (Attwood and Wieland, 2015; Cai et al., 2014; Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Attwood and Wieland, 2015; Cai et al., 2014; Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009.

claim: Histidine phosphorylation of the transient receptor potential vanilloid-5 (TRPV5) channel by NDPKs has been reported.
source: In addition to KCa3.1, histidine phosphorylation of several mammalian proteins by NDPKs has been reported, including the β subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins and the transient receptor potential vanilloid-5 (TRPV5) channel (Attwood and Wieland, 2015; Cai et al., 2014; Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Attwood and Wieland, 2015; Cai et al., 2014; Klumpp and Krieglstein, 2009.

claim: Histidine is a common ligand in metal-ion coordination.
source: The special role of histidine in KCa3.1 inhibition, together with the knowledge that histidine is a common ligand in metal-ion coordination
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical properties of histidine.

claim: Addition of 20 µM TPEN to 293-KCa3.1 cells markedly increased the measured current.
source: As shown in Figure 1A,B,E, the addition of 20 µM TPEN to the cell bath markedly increased the measured current from these cells
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B,E.

claim: The TPEN-induced current increase in 293-KCa3.1 cells was largely blocked by 1 µM TRAM-34.
source: We identified the KCa3.1-mediated current as a major contributor to the current from these cells since it was largely blocked by 1 µM TRAM-34, a KCa3.1-specific inhibitor (Wulff et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Wulff et al., 2000.

claim: TRAM-34 is a KCa3.1-specific inhibitor.
source: since it was largely blocked by 1 µM TRAM-34, a KCa3.1-specific inhibitor (Wulff et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wulff et al., 2000.

claim: TPEN is a high-affinity chelator (KD < 10–10) of several metal ions, including zinc, copper, iron, nickel and manganese.
source: TPEN is a high-affinity chelator (KD < 10–10) of several metal ions, including zinc, copper, iron, nickel and manganese (Smith and Martell, 1975; Treves et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smith and Martell, 1975; Treves et al., 1994.

claim: Addition of 100 µM zinc (ZnCl2) did not alter substantially the measured current from 293-KCa3.1 cells.
source: Addition of 100 µM zinc (ZnCl2) did not alter substantially the measured current from 293-KCa3.1 cells (Figure 1A,E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,E.

claim: Addition of 100 µM copper (CuCl2) to 293-KCa3.1 cells caused a rapid decrease in the current.
source: but addition of 100 µM copper (CuCl2) to the bath caused a rapid decrease in the current (Figure 1B,E), consistent with channel inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,E.

claim: Addition of 20 µM TTM to 293-KCa3.1 cells caused a substantial increase in the measured current.
source: Similar to TPEN, addition of 20 µM TTM to 293-KCa3.1 cells caused a substantial increase in the measured current, which was reversed by the addition of 100 µM CuCl2 (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,E.

claim: The TTM-induced current increase in 293-KCa3.1 cells was reversed by the addition of 100 µM CuCl2.
source: Similar to TPEN, addition of 20 µM TTM to 293-KCa3.1 cells caused a substantial increase in the measured current, which was reversed by the addition of 100 µM CuCl2 (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,E.

claim: TTM is a copper-selective chelator.
source: Because copper but not zinc inhibited KCa3.1 when added to cells, we also tested the copper-selective chelator tetrathiomolybdate (TTM) (Brewer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brewer et al., 2006.

claim: TPEN did not activate substantially KCa3.1 H358N.
source: In contrast to wild-type (WT) KCa3.1, TPEN did not activate substantially, nor did copper inhibit substantially, KCa3.1 H358N (Figure 1D,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: Copper did not inhibit substantially KCa3.1 H358N.
source: In contrast to wild-type (WT) KCa3.1, TPEN did not activate substantially, nor did copper inhibit substantially, KCa3.1 H358N (Figure 1D,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: Copper inhibition of KCa3.1 is strictly dependent on His358.
source: demonstrating that copper inhibition of KCa3.1 is strictly dependent on His358.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the H358N mutant is not inhibited by copper.

claim: Addition of 20 µM TTM to inside-out patches from 293-KCa3.1 cells activated KCa3.1.
source: We first determined whether the addition of 20 µM TTM to the bath could activate KCa3.1, which it did (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of 10 µM copper (CuCl2) to inside-out patches decreased KCa3.1 current to the basal level.
source: We then added 10 µM copper (CuCl2) to the bath, which decreased the current to the basal level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Re-application of TTM activated copper-inhibited KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: Re-application of TTM activated the channel (Figure 2A), demonstrating that inhibition and activation by copper and TTM, respectively, are reversible.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Inhibition and activation of KCa3.1 by copper and TTM, respectively, are reversible.
source: Re-application of TTM activated the channel (Figure 2A), demonstrating that inhibition and activation by copper and TTM, respectively, are reversible.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reversible effects.

claim: NDPK-B activated copper-inhibited KCa3.1 to a similar extent as TTM in inside-out patches.
source: NDPK-B also activated copper-inhibited KCa3.1, to a similar extent as TTM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NDPK-B required GTP to be present to activate KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: However, while NDPK-B required GTP to be present to activate KCa3.1 (Figure 2C), as GTP (or ATP) is necessary for NDPK-B to phosphorylate His358
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TTM did not require GTP to activate KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: TTM did not require GTP to activate KCa3.1 (Figure 2A,B), consistent with TTM simply chelating copper from His358.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Addition of 1 µM TRAM-34 suppressed channel activity to the basal level in all inside-out patch experiments.
source: Addition of 1 µM TRAM-34 suppressed channel activity to the basal level in all I/O patch experiments (Figure 2A–D,F), confirming that the measured activity is due to KCa3.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D,F.

claim: Addition of TTM after treatment with TRAM-34 did not increase the current in inside-out patches from 293-KCa3.1 cells.
source: The TTM-mediated current increase in the I/O patches was further confirmed to be KCa3.1-specific by demonstrating that addition of TTM after treatment with TRAM-34 did not increase the current (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither TTM nor NDPK-B elicited an increase in current in inside-out patches isolated from parental (non-KCa3.1-transfected) 293 cells.
source: as well as by the inability of either TTM or NDPK-B to elicit an increase in current in I/O patches isolated from parental (non-KCa3.1-transfected) 293 cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Copper did not inhibit KCa3.1 channel activity following prior activation by NDPK-B in inside-out patches.
source: We found that copper did not inhibit KCa3.1 channel activity following prior activation by NDPK-B (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation of the imidazole ring of His358 abrogates copper binding.
source: We found that copper did not inhibit KCa3.1 channel activity following prior activation by NDPK-B (Figure 2C), which would be predicted if phosphorylation of the imidazole ring of His358 abrogates copper binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that copper cannot inhibit phosphorylated KCa3.1.

claim: Copper can inhibit a TTM-activated KCa3.1 channel in inside-out patches.
source: This is in contrast to the ability of copper to inhibit a TTM-activated channel (Figure 2A,B), in which case copper is free to bind to His358 once TTM is removed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Addition of TTM did not lead to further activation of NDPK-B-activated KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: Moreover, the addition of TTM did not lead to further activation of KCa3.1 (Figure 2C), as there should be little or no remaining His358-bound copper for TTM to chelate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 10 µM CuCl2 was required to inhibit KCa3.1 in an inside-out patch in the presence of EGTA.
source: While 10 µM CuCl2 was required to inhibit KCa3.1 in an I/O patch in the presence of EGTA, 100 nM CuCl2 was sufficient to inhibit in the absence of EGTA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 100 nM CuCl2 was sufficient to inhibit KCa3.1 in an inside-out patch in the absence of EGTA.
source: While 10 µM CuCl2 was required to inhibit KCa3.1 in an I/O patch in the presence of EGTA, 100 nM CuCl2 was sufficient to inhibit in the absence of EGTA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EGTA chelates copper.
source: In addition to chelating calcium, EGTA also chelates copper (Xiao and Wedd, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xiao and Wedd, 2010.

claim: The ability of copper to inhibit KCa3.1 is inversely dependent on the calcium concentration.
source: Furthermore, the ability of copper to inhibit KCa3.1 is inversely dependent on the calcium concentration: approximately 1 µM CuCl2 was required for inhibition at 10 µM CaCl2 (Figure 2E), versus 100 nM CuCl2 at 300 nM CaCl2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Approximately 1 µM CuCl2 was required for inhibition of KCa3.1 at 10 µM CaCl2 in inside-out patches.
source: approximately 1 µM CuCl2 was required for inhibition at 10 µM CaCl2 (Figure 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The copper-inhibited current and TRAM-34-inhibited current in 10 µM calcium were the same in inside-out patches.
source: The copper (Figure 2E) and TRAM-34-inhibited currents (Figure 2F) in 10 µM calcium, following the addition of TTM, were the same, indicating that the copper-inhibited current is specific to KCa3.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Activation of KCa3.1 requires both His358 phosphorylation by NDPK-B and calcium binding to KCa3.1-bound calmodulin.
source: We showed previously that activation of KCa3.1 requires both His358 phosphorylation by NDPK-B and calcium binding to KCa3.1-bound calmodulin (Srivastava et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Addition of 20 µM TTM to an inside-out patch in low calcium (30 nM) did not result in KCa3.1 activation.
source: Addition of 20 µM TTM to an I/O patch in low calcium (30 nM) did not result in KCa3.1 activation (Figure 3A), indicating that calcium is also required for TTM activation of KCa3.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Calcium is required for TTM activation of KCa3.1.
source: Addition of 20 µM TTM to an I/O patch in low calcium (30 nM) did not result in KCa3.1 activation (Figure 3A), indicating that calcium is also required for TTM activation of KCa3.1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no activation in low calcium.

claim: Addition of 300 nM calcium to an inside-out patch following 20 µM TTM did not activate KCa3.1.
source: Surprisingly, addition of 300 nM calcium to an I/O patch following 20 µM TTM did not activate KCa3.1, although it did activate other non-KCa3.1 channels that were not inhibited by TRAM-34 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TTM and high calcium needed to be present simultaneously for activation of KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: Rather, TTM and high calcium needed to be present simultaneously for activation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NDPK-B and high calcium needed to be present simultaneously for activation of KCa3.1 in inside-out patches.
source: A similar result was obtained for activation of KCa3.1 by NDPK-B (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A calcium/calmodulin-induced conformational change in the channel is required for TTM and NDPK-B to gain access to copper and His358, respectively.
source: These data suggest that a calcium/calmodulin-induced conformational change in the channel is required for TTM and NDPK-B to gain access to copper and His358, respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that calcium and TTM/NDPK-B must be present simultaneously.

claim: Addition of copper inhibited the TRAM-34-sensitive current, but not the current from other channels activated by calcium in inside-out patches.
source: Addition of copper inhibited the TRAM-34-sensitive current, but not the current from other channels activated by calcium (Figure 3A), providing further evidence that copper specifically inhibits KCa3.1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The basal current is approximately three-fold higher in KCa3.1-transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs than in transfected WT MEFs.
source: As shown in Figure 4A–C, the basal current is approximately three-fold higher in the KCa3.1-transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs than in the transfected WT MEFs expressing similar amounts of GFP-KCa3.1
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Addition of 20 µM TTM had little effect on the current from KCa3.1-transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the transfected WT MEFs (Figure 4A,C), addition of 20 µM TTM had little effect on the current from the transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Addition of exogenous copper (10 µM) inhibited KCa3.1 current in transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs as well as WT MEFs.
source: Addition of exogenous copper (10 µM) inhibited KCa3.1 current in the transfected Ctr1-/- MEFs as well as the WT MEFs (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Entry of copper into Ctr1-/- MEFs was presumably mediated by a Ctr1-independent process.
source: Entry of copper into Ctr1-/- MEFs was presumably mediated by a Ctr1-independent process, as has been described (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that copper can enter Ctr1-/- cells, supported by citation to Lee et al., 2002.

claim: The failure of exogenous TTM to increase KCa3.1 current in WT MEFs to levels similar to those in Ctr1-/- MEFs is likely due to incomplete chelation of copper bound to His358.
source: The failure of exogenous TTM to increase KCa3.1 current in WT MEFs to levels similar to those in Ctr1-/- MEFs (Figure 4A,B) is likely due to incomplete chelation of copper bound to His358.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing incomplete activation by TTM.

claim: The surface levels of KCa3.1 in WT and Ctr1-/- MEFs were very similar.
source: FACS analysis of non-permeabilized cells demonstrated that the surface levels of KCa3.1 in the two types of MEFs were very similar (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Endogenous KCa3.1 channel activity was markedly increased in CD4+ T cells isolated from Ctr1+/- mice compared to those from WT littermate controls.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, endogenous KCa3.1 channel activity was markedly increased in CD4+ T cells isolated from Ctr1+/- mice compared to those from WT littermate controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The level of cytoplasmic copper in Ctr1+/- splenocytes is approximately 50% of that in WT splenocytes.
source: The level of cytoplasmic copper in the Ctr1+/- splenocytes is approximately 50% of that in WT splenocytes (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2001.

claim: Histidine phosphorylation of endogenous KCa3.1 was significantly increased in T cells from Ctr1+/- mice versus those from WT littermate controls.
source: Consistent with increased KCa3.1 activity, by blotting with a monoclonal antibody specific for 3-pHis (Fuhs et al., 2015), we observed significantly increased histidine phosphorylation of (endogenous) KCa3.1 in T cells from Ctr1+/- mice versus those from WT littermate controls
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to Fuhs et al., 2015.

claim: There was no appreciable difference in KCa3.1 expression levels between T cells from Ctr1+/- mice and WT littermate controls.
source: with no appreciable difference in KCa3.1 expression levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: T-cell receptor-stimulated calcium influx was substantially increased in Ctr1+/- T cells.
source: In accord with elevated KCa3.1 activity, T-cell receptor-stimulated (by anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies) calcium influx and cytokine production—interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα)—were also substantially increased in Ctr1+/- T cells (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: T-cell receptor-stimulated cytokine production (IL-2, IFN-γ and TNFα) was substantially increased in Ctr1+/- T cells.
source: In accord with elevated KCa3.1 activity, T-cell receptor-stimulated (by anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies) calcium influx and cytokine production—interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα)—were also substantially increased in Ctr1+/- T cells (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Copper (Cu(II)) is found to be coordinated solely by four histidine residues.
source: Of the metal ions listed above, only copper (Cu(II)) is found to be coordinated solely by four histidine residues (Dokmanić et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dokmanić et al., 2008.

claim: The BK and Shaker potassium channels have been shown to be inhibited by copper.
source: Although the BK and Shaker potassium channels and TASK-3, a two-pore-domain potassium channel, have also been shown to be inhibited by copper (Gruss et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gruss et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2008.

claim: TASK-3, a two-pore-domain potassium channel, has been shown to be inhibited by copper.
source: Although the BK and Shaker potassium channels and TASK-3, a two-pore-domain potassium channel, have also been shown to be inhibited by copper (Gruss et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gruss et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2008.

claim: The copper inhibition mechanism in BK, Shaker, and TASK-3 channels is distinct from that in KCa3.1 because copper acts extracellularly in these other channels.
source: the inhibition mechanism is distinct from that in KCa3.1 because copper acts extracellularly in these other channels, and there is no evidence that these effects are regulated by histidine phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of copper inhibition mechanisms.

claim: His358 is located just C-terminal to the calmodulin-binding domain in KCa3.1.
source: His358 is located just C-terminal to the calmodulin-binding domain in KCa3.1 and 18 residues N-terminal to the predicted C-terminal coiled-coil region
evidence: This is a structural description of the protein.

claim: His358 is 18 residues N-terminal to the predicted C-terminal coiled-coil region in KCa3.1.
source: His358 is located just C-terminal to the calmodulin-binding domain in KCa3.1 and 18 residues N-terminal to the predicted C-terminal coiled-coil region
evidence: This is a structural description of the protein.

claim: Crystallographic analysis shows that the C-terminal coiled-coil region of KCa3.1 forms a four-helix bundle.
source: which crystallographic analysis shows forms a four-helix bundle (S.R.H., unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished crystallographic data from the authors.

claim: There is a reasonable probability that the region encompassing His358 forms a coiled-coil/four-helix bundle.
source: Coiled-coil prediction software indicates that there is a reasonable probability that the region encompassing His358 also forms a coiled-coil/four-helix bundle
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction.

claim: His358 occupies an inward-facing 'a' position in the heptad repeat of the predicted coiled-coil.
source: with His358 occupying an inward-facing 'a' position in the heptad repeat, which would position the four copies of His358 to coordinate a copper ion (via N3 in the imidazole ring) on the four-fold axis.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction and structural modeling.

claim: The four copies of His358 would be positioned to coordinate a copper ion (via N3 in the imidazole ring) on the four-fold axis.
source: with His358 occupying an inward-facing 'a' position in the heptad repeat, which would position the four copies of His358 to coordinate a copper ion (via N3 in the imidazole ring) on the four-fold axis.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction and structural modeling.

claim: In the absence of calcium (basal state), copper binding to the four copies of His358 in homotetrameric KCa3.1 maintains low channel activity by opposing the calcium/calmodulin-mediated conformational changes that induce channel opening.
source: In the absence of calcium (basal state), copper binding to the four copies of His358 in homotetrameric KCa3.1 maintains low channel activity by opposing the calcium/calmodulin-mediated conformational changes that induce channel opening.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Upon a marked increase in intracellular calcium levels, calcium binding to channel-associated calmodulin induces conformational changes in the channel.
source: Upon a marked increase in intracellular calcium levels due to T-cell stimulation (for example), calcium binding to channel-associated calmodulin induces conformational changes in the channel
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Calcium-induced conformational changes distort the four-helix bundle locally and partially destabilize copper binding to His358.
source: distorting the four-helix bundle locally (the C-terminal four-helix bundle is maintained) and partially destabilizing copper binding to His358, thus exposing it to phosphorylation by NDPK-B.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Phosphorylation of a single His358 residue in the tetramer is probably sufficient to abrogate copper binding.
source: Because stable copper binding requires tetravalent coordination, phosphorylation of a single His358 residue (on N3) in the tetramer is probably sufficient to abrogate copper binding and inhibition of KCa3.1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on chemical reasoning.

claim: Stable copper binding requires tetravalent coordination.
source: Because stable copper binding requires tetravalent coordination
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper coordination chemistry.

claim: The TRPV5 calcium channel is activated by NDPK-B-mediated histidine phosphorylation.
source: Although our model for KCa3.1 inhibition and activation might be unique for a potassium channel, we recently demonstrated that the TRPV5 calcium channel is also activated by NDPK-B-mediated histidine phosphorylation (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Copper chelators such as penicillamine were able to slow growth of oncogenic BRAFV600E-driven tumors in mice, through inactivation of MEK1.
source: It was recently shown that copper chelators such as penicillamine, used to treat Wilson disease (copper-overload disorder), were able to slow growth of oncogenic BRAFV600E-driven tumors in mice, through inactivation of MEK1 (Brady et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brady et al., 2014.

claim: Treatment of patients harboring BRAFV600E driven-tumors with copper chelators has the potential to not only block BRAF activation of the MAP kinase pathway, but also to enhance T-cell-mediated killing of these tumors via enhanced activation of KCa3.1.
source: Thus, treatment of patients harboring BRAFV600E driven-tumors with copper chelators has the potential to not only block BRAF activation of the MAP kinase pathway, but also to enhance T-cell-mediated killing of these tumors via enhanced activation of KCa3.1.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication based on the findings.

claim: Ctr1-/- mice are embryonically lethal.
source: Because Ctr1-/- mice are embryonically lethal, we assessed T-cell activation in CD4+ T cells from mice that were heterozygous for Ctr1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ctr1 knockout mouse model.

claim: KCa3.1 with an exofacial HA epitope tag inserted into the extracellular loop between transmembrane helices S3 and S4 functions normally.
source: Previous studies (Srivastava et al., 2005; Syme et al., 2003) have demonstrated that KCa3.1 with this tag functions normally and can be specifically detected at the plasma membrane following staining of non-permeabilized cells with anti-HA antibody.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Srivastava et al., 2005; Syme et al., 2003.
